To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the power-law distribution of rupture events is a consequence of the progressive failure in heterogeneous materials and that the variations in the slope of the distribution are due to the proximity to the critical point.
(i) the power law is a universal feature of rupture event distributions and (ii) its slope and tail shape are strongly affected by the distance to critical point.
the variability of the power-law distribution of rupture events observed in nature and in experiments is explained by the critical point theory.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the variability of power-law distributions in rupture phenomena and the identification of the factors responsible for this variability.
the understanding of the variability of rupture event distributions in heterogeneous materials and the identification of the physical factors responsible for this variability.
the statistical analysis of the rupture event sizes and with the identification of the factors controlling the variability of their distributions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rupture events obeying power-law distributions are ubiquitous but their slope and tail-shape are not universal.
the rupture event size distributions are not universal, and the slope and the shape are sensitive to various factors.
the power-law distribution of rupture event sizes is a general characteristic of the deformation process in heterogeneous media.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the critical point theory can be used to explain the variations in rupture events distributions, however, the proximity of the system to the critical point is not the only factor that controls these variations.
the critical point theory can explain a part of power-law variability, but the role of heterogeneity and stress is also crucial.
the critical point theory can be used to predict the power-law distributions and its variations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the power-law variability can be attributed to the proximity to the brittle/ductile critical point.
the critical point theory provides a unified framework for understanding power-law variability observed for various rupture events.
the criticality of rupture events is the key factor to understand power-law variability.
